hero.subtitle: Securing the web by layering HTTP over TLS, establishing the foundation for all secure web communication.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP Over TLS (commonly known as HTTPS) provides a mechanism for securing HTTP connections using TLS (Transport Layer Security). This is the cornerstone of web security, enabling encrypted communication between browsers and servers.

HTTPS is simply HTTP layered on top of TLS/SSL. The protocol itself is not different from HTTP; it uses TLS to encrypt the entire HTTP conversation.

Default Port
HTTPS uses port 443 instead of HTTP's port 80
URI Scheme
URLs use the https:// scheme identifier

sections.title: Connection Initiation
sections.content:
The client initiates a TLS connection to the server on port 443. Once the TLS handshake is complete, the client sends its first HTTP request. All HTTP data is sent as TLS application data.

sections.title: Endpoint Identification
sections.content:
The client must verify the server's identity using the certificate presented during the TLS handshake. The hostname in the URI must match the identity in the server's certificate.

If the hostname does not match the certificate, the client MUST either notify the user or terminate the connection. This prevents man-in-the-middle attacks.

Certificate matching rules:

dNSNameMatch against the hostname using wildcard rules
iPAddressMatch against the host IP if connecting by IP
Common NameLegacy fallback if no SubjectAltName extension

sections.title: Impact on the Modern Web
sections.content:
HTTPS has become the de facto standard for all web communication. Major browsers now flag HTTP sites as "Not Secure," and search engines prioritize HTTPS sites in rankings.

Let's Encrypt
Free, automated certificates have driven HTTPS adoption to over 95% of web traffic
HSTS
HTTP Strict Transport Security (RFC 6797) forces HTTPS-only connections
Mixed Content
Browsers block insecure resources loaded on HTTPS pages
